The CNPD opened an investigation into a Luxembourg manufacturer of technical equipment, focusing on its record of processing activities under Article 30 GDPR, and carried out an on-site visit in November 2023. The restricted committee found the record incomplete, imprecise, inconsistent and incorrect, notably on recipients and on transfers to third countries. It treated this as a single infringement of Article 30(1)(a), (c), (d) and (e), of low gravity and falling under Article 83(4). It issued a reprimand, ordered the company to correct the record within two months, and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 7,000.

An NHS GP surgery sent 23 years of a patient's medical records to the patient's insurer, when the insurer had asked for only five years and the patient had asked to review the records first. The Commissioner found infringements of the data minimisation principle (Article 5(1)(c)), the integrity and confidentiality principle with Article 32 security of processing (Articles 5(1)(f) and 32), and late breach notification (Article 33), which was reported 26 days after the surgery became aware of it. The Commissioner issued a reprimand under Article 58(2)(b) UK GDPR and imposed no fine. The Commissioner found that the surgery had remedied the infringements by February 2025.

A lawyer complained that the Rechtsanwaltskammer gave an incomplete access response under Article 15 GDPR, omitting the disciplinary lawyer's statement and the chamber's communications with that lawyer. The DSB dismissed the complaint: Article 15(3) gives a right to a copy of personal data, not to copies of whole documents, and the chamber's and the other lawyer's confidentiality interests outweighed the request, with Article 23 restrictions as a fallback. The decision is not final; the complainant lodged an appeal to the Federal Administrative Court.

In 2021 a hacker used SQL injection through a web form to reach a database server of the HAN university and demanded a ransom. The Dutch DPA investigated not the breach itself but whether the security measures before it were adequate. It found they were not appropriate to the risk, so Article 32 GDPR was infringed. It set a base fine of EUR 310,000 under its 2019 fining guidelines and reduced it to EUR 175,000 because of the HAN's mitigation efforts, an information security project already under way, and its outreach to other organisations. The HAN admitted the infringement and, according to the press release, will not object.

The ICO found that Police Scotland, when preparing misconduct packs, breached the Data Protection Act 2018 (sections 35 and 37) in its mobile phone data extraction. It also breached the UK GDPR on security, data minimisation, data protection by design and breach notification. In one incident, a complainant's mobile phone extraction data was wrongly disclosed to a third party, and the breach was not reported within 72 hours. The ICO issued a reprimand for the DPA infringements and a single penalty of £66,000 for the UK GDPR infringements. The public sector approach meant no fine for the DPA infringements, although the ICO had initially considered one of £78,750.

Deezer notified the CNIL of a data breach in November 2022 that pointed to its former processor, Mobius Solutions (Optimove), an Israeli marketing-tool company with no EU establishment. After an inspection, the CNIL's restricted committee held that the GDPR applies under Article 3(2)(b) because the company's segmentation of Deezer users amounts to behavioural profiling. It found breaches of Articles 28, 29 and 30 GDPR. It fined the company EUR 1,000,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with the company no longer named after two years.
The DPA fined a company GBP 105,000 (approximately €120,000) for sending over 67 million unsolicited direct marketing emails to data subjects without consent or a valid exception.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation in November 2025 into Crowd Entertainment Limited after a data subject complained about how their access request was handled. The operator could not show it had given a complete and proper written reply within the legal time limit, covering the complainant's player accounts on its platforms and information on self-exclusion requests. It was fined 76,333 lei (about EUR 15,000) and ordered to give a full reply to the request and to put in place technical and organisational measures, including staff training and involvement of the DPO, so that data subject requests are handled correctly and on time.

The DPA reprimanded and fined a university €98,000 following six data breaches after it failed to take appropriate measures to ensure security of processing, to keep a record of processing activities, and to comply with its notification obligations.

Three complainants said the Belgian federal public health service's medical expertise unit (Medex) lost or misplaced their paper medical files while they were being transferred between regional and central offices for a military disability pension assessment. The Chamber found the files contained health data and that Medex may have breached the security, accountability and breach-notification provisions of the GDPR. Because the Chamber treated the decision as a prima facie decision, it adopted a warning rather than a fine, and it noted that the inspection and Medex's later measures had addressed the problem. The breach of the notification duty was tied to only one of the lost files, which Medex had not notified.

The Romanian DPA completed an investigation in November 2025 at a water company after a customer complained that an employee had disclosed the customer's personal data on a social network. It found that the company had not adopted sufficient security measures to protect its clients' data. The company was fined RON 5,084 (EUR 1,000) and ordered to bring its processing into compliance, including regular training of people with access to personal data and involving the data protection officer.

The Slovenian Information Commissioner, acting ex officio, issued a misdemeanour decision against a company and its responsible person. The website's online forms (service orders, account registration and login, contact and comment forms) collected personal data, but the information required by Article 13 GDPR was not accessible in a suitable way when the data was collected. The Commissioner found breaches of Articles 12(1) and 13 GDPR and imposed fines of EUR 4,800 on the legal entity and EUR 300 on the responsible person.

A school institute in Casalecchio di Reno published on its official website a teacher ranking list containing about 1,333 teachers' residential addresses, personal emails, phone numbers and tax codes, due to an administrative assistant's mistake, over roughly two years. After a complaint the school removed the list from its site, but a third-party website kept it online. The Garante found that the publication was unlawful under GDPR Article 5(1)(a) and (c) and Article 6(1)(c) and (e), and Article 2-ter of the Italian Privacy Code, and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 plus publication of the order on the Garante's website. No further corrective measures were ordered because the school's conduct had already run its course.

A complainant said the municipality of Tuscania ran about 50 street cameras, with licence-plate reading, plus cameras at waste collection points, with no signage or full privacy notice. The municipality had also refused an access request and had not signed processor agreements. The Garante found that the urban-security pact with the Prefecture did not identify the cameras or areas covered, so there was no valid legal basis. It also found transparency failures, no DPIA, no Article 28 arrangements, an unlawful refusal of access, and incomplete compliance with an earlier Garante order. It fined the municipality EUR 12,000 in total for two separate conducts and ordered it to stop processing and delete the plate data and to review all its cameras.

A school's ordinary (non-restricted) administrative protocol register held a court filing from a former employee in a labour dispute with the school. The filing contained health data and was visible to administrative staff and to the headmaster's collaborators, who had no need to see it. The employee complained, the school moved the file to the restricted register within about 24 hours of the complaint, and the school admitted a material error. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a), 6, 9(2)(b) and (g), 13 and 29 GDPR and the related Italian Code provisions, and imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 for the unitary conduct. The decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

A school institute sent a reminder email about compulsory vaccination documents for pupils under 16 to about 36-37 parents, with all recipients' email addresses visible in the To field instead of blind copy. The complaint came from parents through their lawyer. The Garante found that the disclosure of email addresses, together with information revealing pupils' vaccination status (health data), had no valid legal basis, and that the school's claim of a material error did not change this. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 and ordered publication of the decision.
The DPA fined a customer support provider €80,000 for unlawfully transferring its employees’ private phone numbers to its business customer without a valid legal basis.
The DPA held that a data subject had manifestly made their health data public by disclosing an ADHD diagnosis on a publicly accessible forum, even though the post was published under a pseudonym.
The DPA fined an adult ad network for placing advertising cookies without consent, unlawfully relying on legitimate interest and lacking an EU representative.

A data subject asked a parking service provider by email, in October 2022, for access to their personal data, but the provider refused to process the request unless they filled in a web form requiring their national identification number. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found that the provider had not granted the access right under Article 15(1) and (3) GDPR, had not facilitated the exercise of rights under Article 12(2), had breached Article 12(6) and the data minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c), and had asked for unnecessary data. The authority issued a reprimand and ordered the provider to comply with the access request, unless it had already done so. No fine was imposed. The decision is final. It is a corrected version, of 3 December 2025, of a decision of 11 November 2025 under the same case number.

The DPA held that the Ministry of Education and Sports of Andalusia’s provision of cloud-based educational services to public schools violated GDPR provisions relating to transparency, privacy by design, international data transfers and DPIA duties. The Ministry used Microsoft as a processor for this activity.

The DPA fined two so-called 'sovereign citizens' and founding members of an organisation providing identity documents for a non-existing state €1,300 each. The organisation processed personal data without a valid legal basis and did not provide data subjects with adequate information.

A former employee complained that his former employer (called Y1 in the decision) gave an incomplete response to his access request under Article 15 GDPR, and that the former employer had no legal basis for passing his references to a prospective employer (called Y2 in the decision), during a job application. The prospective employer was also complained about for a late and incomplete reply to the same access request. The Litigation Chamber held that employment references about a person are personal data and that sharing them during a reference check is processing. It found the former employer in breach of Articles 6(1), 12(2) to (4) and 15(1) and (3) GDPR, and the prospective employer in breach of Article 12(3) GDPR. Both were given a reprimand, with no fine.

A sports retailer notified the Spanish DPA of a ransomware intrusion in October 2023 that encrypted critical machines and led to data exfiltration, affecting about 6.2 million people. The AEPD opened a sanction procedure for failing to apply appropriate security measures (Art. 5(1)(f) GDPR) and proposed a fine of EUR 2,600,000. The company acknowledged responsibility and paid voluntarily on 5 November 2025, which earned two cumulative 20% reductions under Article 85 LPACAP. The AEPD therefore confirmed the infringement, set the final fine at EUR 1,560,000 and closed the procedure. It also ordered the company to report within 6 months the security measures set out in the initiation agreement.

After inspections in January 2023, the CNIL restricted committee found that American Express Carte France breached the cookie and tracker rules in Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act. The company set trackers without consent or despite refusal, and did not make withdrawal of consent effective. The committee also addressed a data minimisation issue under Article 5(1)(c) GDPR concerning telephone call recordings. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,500,000 for the Article 82 breach and ordered publication of the decision, with the company no longer named after two years. It issued no injunction because the company had come into compliance during the procedure.

A complainant objected to the sale of his personal data for direct marketing. The data broker Infobel had obtained the data from another source and passed it on through a media agency to a marketing company. The Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber found that Infobel could not show valid consent, and therefore no valid legal basis, for processing the data, in breach of Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1) and 24 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 40,000 and ordered erasure of the data and notice to recipients. The Cour des marchés later partly annulled the decision, including the erasure and notice orders, and set the fine at EUR 5,000 on full review.

After a cyberattack, an accounting practice lost control of its IT infrastructure and the personal data of a significant number of people was accessed and disclosed without authorisation. The practice had notified the breach under Article 33. The authority found that it had not put in place technical and organisational measures appropriate to the risk. It fined the practice RON 10,167, equivalent to EUR 2,000, for breaching Article 32(1)(b) and (2) GDPR.

The Italian DPA examined a complaint and a later report from a former and a prospective customer of a home security company who kept receiving promotional SMS and calls after asking for erasure and objecting to marketing. It found that the company answered the rights requests late, collected invalid consent for marketing through its website quote box, and breached storage limitation and information duties on retention periods. It fined the company EUR 400,000 (0.18% of turnover), ordered a ban on marketing use of the data obtained without valid consent, deletion of that data, and corrected privacy notices. Publication of the decision was ordered as an ancillary sanction. Some complaints, on telebooking and former-customer legal bases, were closed.

The Italian DPA investigated Aimag S.p.A., a water and waste utility, after a report that anyone could register on its website's customer area using only a tax code and any email address, with no identity check. The inspection also found pre-ticked consent boxes for marketing, unclear privacy notices and a five-year retention period for marketing data. The Garante found violations of security, lawful basis, transparency and storage-limitation rules. It ordered Aimag to adopt adequate security measures and to update its consent wording and privacy notice, and imposed a fine of EUR 300,000 plus publication of the decision.

A complaint concerned a questionnaire for a university research project about a residential cooperative, sent to its residents and hosted on a grant holder's personal Google Form. The questionnaire asked for identifying details and special-category data such as political opinions and blood donation, with no prior information and no valid legal basis. The Garante declared the University of Turin's processing unlawful, found breaches of the principles, transparency, accountability, privacy by design, security and staff instructions, and issued a reprimand because the data had been deleted, about 10 people were affected, and the breach was non-intentional. It also ordered publication of the decision on its website.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in October 2025 into Cucina di Fabio S.R.L. after a complaint about unsolicited commercial emails sent without consent. The controller processed the complainant's email address for direct marketing without proof of consent. It also collected email addresses and sent marketing messages without checking that the addresses came from their users and that recipients had expressly consented. The authority imposed two fines (1,000 and 2,000 euro equivalent) and ordered corrective measures so that direct marketing emails are sent only with prior express consent.

The Slovenian Information Commissioner issued a misdemeanour decision against a legal entity providing public utility services and against its responsible person. The company had installed GPS transmitters in service vehicles used by its employees and, over a period of time, systematically and indiscriminately collected location data on employees and their complete routes, without any legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR. The breach of the principle of lawfulness under Article 5(1)(a) GDPR was found, and fines were imposed: EUR 6,000 on the legal entity and EUR 600 on the responsible person.

A job applicant complained that the company did not tell him it was keeping his application documents to defend possible legal claims, and that it passed them to a second respondent, a law firm, and refused erasure. The authority held that the company could keep the CV for seven months after the rejection under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR (defence against claims under the equal treatment law) and keep the other documents to defend legal claims under Article 17(3)(e) GDPR. It dismissed the complaint against both respondents. The decision is not final: an appeal to the Federal Administrative Court (BVwG) is pending.

A customer complained that the online shop's registration process forced a choice of 'Herr' or 'Frau' as salutation and linked it to the account. The authority found that the controller violated the Art. 5 principles of purpose limitation and data minimisation, because the salutation was not necessary for the contract or any other stated purpose, and Art. 6(1)(b) and (f) could not justify it. During the procedure the controller switched to gender-neutral registration, so the authority issued no order. The complaints on rectification and erasure were closed informally after the controller complied, and the Art. 25 complaint about privacy-friendly defaults was dismissed. No fine was imposed. The decision is final.

The DPA held that the deletion of personal data by the controller during the proceedings constituted a violation of the data subject's right of access under Article 15 in conjunction with Article 5(1)(a) GDPR.

The Slovenian supervisory authority issued a misdemeanour decision on its own initiative. A publicly accessible web server held registration confirmations with personal data (name, address, year of birth, email, phone number, shirt size) of 12 registrants. The documents could be reached through unique URLs with no further protection, and the URLs were not generated with enough randomness, so an average user could reach them by guessing sequential codes. The authority found a breach of the Art. 32 security obligation and fined the legal entity EUR 16,250 and its responsible person EUR 400.

The DPA refused to handle a complaint filed by a data subject against the court-appointed expert who prepared an opinion on contract arrangement in a joint custody case. According to the DPA, the complaint was abusive since it was aimed to delegitimize the expert’s work rather than data protection reasons.

Following a second complaint from the NOYB association, the CNIL carried out online inspections of the Vanity Fair website run by Les Publications Condé Nast. It found that the company placed an advertising cookie (NID) before any consent, and that the cookie banner gave wrong information about cookies presented as strictly necessary. Other shortcomings concerned the collection of consent and the handling of refusal and withdrawal. The restricted committee fined the company EUR 750,000 for breaching Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act and ordered the decision published, with the company no longer named after two years.

The ICO fined LastPass UK Ltd £1,228,283 under the UK GDPR after two linked security incidents in 2022 in which a threat actor reached the company's backup database holding customer data. The ICO found that LastPass let senior staff reach corporate credentials from personal devices and encouraged linking of employee business and personal accounts. It held these practices were not appropriate technical and organisational measures under Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1). About 1.63 million UK data subjects were affected. The ICO treated the case as serious but, in setting the amount, took account of the sophisticated attack and the company's zero-knowledge encryption of vault contents.

Two complainants (a son and his mother) complained that municipal employees had consulted their National Register data in December 2019 for private purposes, and that the commune's replies were unsatisfactory. The Inspectorate found that the commune had no adequate control mechanism to ensure its staff accessed the register only for authorised purposes. The Chamber Contentieuse held that the employees were personally responsible for their unlawful consultations, so those were not attributed to the commune, but that the commune still breached Articles 5(2) and 24(1) GDPR. It issued a reprimand, not a fine, because Belgian law does not allow administrative fines on public authorities.

The Romanian authority ANSPDCP investigated Greencorp S.R.L. after the company notified a personal data breach. A cyberattack had encrypted its database of employee data and disrupted its IT system. The investigation found the company lacked security measures specific enough to prevent such an attack, breaching Article 32(1)(b) and (d) read with Article 32(2) GDPR. It imposed a fine of 15,258 lei (stated as about EUR 3,000) and ordered the company to introduce multi-factor authentication and password complexity rules for remote accounts.

The DPA fined a journalist €80 for unlawfully disclosing the identity of a data subject on the journalist’s social media profile after the data subject had reported them for a parking violation at a Christmas market.

IMY opened a supervision case in June 2025 into how the Swedish Social Insurance Agency handles personal data in risk-based selection for targeted checks on temporary parental benefit claims, including any use of an AI system. The agency said it had used a machine-learning risk profile but withdrew it a little over a month before its reply, and that it has no plans to reinstate it. IMY found the processing under review had ceased and closed the case without further investigation. No infringement was found and no corrective measure was imposed.

After a cyberattack gave unauthorised access to personal data of many employees, clients and collaborators (identification data, salaries, bank accounts) and restricted the controller's access to its own IT infrastructure, the Romanian authority investigated following the controller's breach notification. It found the controller had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures nor regularly tested their effectiveness. It fined the controller RON 40,663 (about EUR 8,000) and ordered it to implement appropriate measures, including multi-factor authentication for remote accounts and a password complexity policy.

The DPA held that a court-appointed psychologist can act as a controller and found a violation of Article 12(3) GDPR because the psychologist failed to respond to a data subject's access request without informing about the reasons for inaction.

The DPA fined a communication network provider €4,500,000 for several GDPR breaches including unlawful data transfers to Serbia and for misleading users with vague information that hid regular third-country processing.

The Garante learned through a report that the municipality of Orte had installed video surveillance cameras without ensuring transparency towards data subjects. The investigation found 43 cameras, operated without a sufficient legal basis, with deficient information notices and no data protection impact assessment, and the municipality also failed to fully and promptly answer the Authority's information requests. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 for the video surveillance conduct and EUR 1,000 for the failure to cooperate, EUR 6,000 in total. No further corrective measures were ordered because the cameras were no longer active, and the order is to be published.

The Romanian authority (ANSPDCP) investigated the courier company Fan Courier Express S.R.L. after a complainant said it had not answered a request to access and erase their data. The investigation found the company did not reply to the request or provide a copy of the data, and that it processed personal data unlawfully by attaching a derogatory remark to the complainant. Two fines were imposed, one for the access and erasure failures and one for the unlawful processing, and corrective measures were ordered. The text is a press release; the decision itself is not reproduced.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation into Whitedecor SRL in October 2025, started by a complaint from an individual. The company repeatedly sent unsolicited marketing messages to a customer's phone after a purchase and could not prove consent. It also did not show it answered the customer's access, objection and erasure requests within one month. The authority imposed two fines of RON 5,082 each (about EUR 1,000 each) and ordered corrective measures on internal procedures for data subject requests and direct marketing consent.

The DPA ordered the operator of a live-streaming website to change their cookie banner due to its deceptive design. The DPA considered the “accept” option to be visually more prominent, unlawfully nudging users towards consent.

Romania's data protection authority, acting as lead authority, investigated Klass Wagen S.R.L. after the company notified a personal data breach and the authority received a referral. A former employee had disclosed colleagues' credentials for the contract management system, which allowed unauthorised access to the personal data of a very large number of customers and employees, including people in other EU/EEA states. The incident was reported late internally, so no immediate measures were taken. The authority found a breach of Art. 32(1)(b) and (d) and (2) GDPR, fined the company 35,615 lei (about EUR 7,000), and ordered it to put in place a procedure for revoking access rights and deactivating former employees' accounts.

A former employee of a business run by a sole trader asked on 30 April 2024 for access to the login and logout records linked to his personal email account on the business's website platform. The controller refused, arguing the data belonged to the business or third parties, that providing it was technically impossible, that it would endanger security, and that the request was abusive because it sought evidence for a lawsuit. The Authority rejected each ground and found a breach of Article 15(1) and 15(3) read with Article 12(5) GDPR. It ordered the controller to give the complainant access to his data and to tell the Authority within one month of being notified of the decision, and imposed a fine of EUR 1,000.

The DPA held that, even though a complaint against a medical doctor, who had allegedly accessed medical files without authorization, was later withdrawn, his failure to cooperate with the DPA still justified issuing a reprimand.

The Spanish AEPD sanctioned the airport operator AENA for running a voluntary facial-recognition system for passengers to access airport areas without a valid data protection impact assessment. The assessment did not justify necessity and proportionality, was not updated, and processing went ahead despite two unfavourable reports from the AEPD. The Agency found an infringement of Article 35 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 10,043,002. It also confirmed the temporary suspension of all biometric processing until AENA carries out a proper impact assessment.

Five complainants, parents and their children, asked the Upper Austrian education directorate to erase their personal data held under school-attendance and education-documentation law. The authority dismissed the complaints of four complainants, because the directorate must keep the data for compulsory schooling (Art. 6(1)(c), Art. 17(3)(b)) and the claimed legal-claims ground was too abstract. For the third complainant, whose nine years of compulsory schooling ended in 2023, it found a violation of the right to erasure and ordered erasure within four weeks.

A State Police inspector used his police access to the MOBAPP application on 21 January 2025, outside working hours and for personal reasons, to obtain a data subject's name, national ID number, date of birth, photo and home address. He passed part of this data (photo, address, date of birth) to a third person, and it was posted in a Discord group the same day. The Latvian data protection authority (DVI) found breaches of GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and (b) and 6(1), and imposed a fine of EUR 150 (30 fine units). The case was decided in written procedure.

A customer complained that the supermarket chain N*** GmbH breached his right to confidentiality by reviewing CCTV footage of him at a checkout after he complained that staff had refused card payment at a till and forced him to pay cash. The company reviewed and then deleted the recordings in order to investigate a suspected coercion offence. The authority held the complaint only just admissible and dismissed it as unfounded, finding the review covered by the surveillance purpose and limited to what was necessary.

At the end of 2024 a large personal data leak affecting almost all Latvian municipalities was found; the data were stored in an information system run by ZZ Dats. The Data State Inspectorate inspected and found that the company breached Article 32 GDPR because it had not sufficiently ensured that processor obligations were met. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 300,000, calculated under the Inspectorate's methodology based on EDPB guidelines. The company has appealed to the Riga City Court. The municipalities involved received reprimands for insufficient oversight of the processor.

The DPA held that a publisher of console games could comply with an access request by providing a user with remote access via their user account. However, the DPA found that information was incomplete and found a violation of Article 15 GDPR.

A medical centre treating infertility mistakenly sent a refund transfer confirmation, whose title named a genetic test indicating advanced prenatal diagnostics, to another patient with the same first name. The controller judged that the incident posed no risk and neither reported it to the UODO nor told the data subject. The UODO President found it was a confidentiality breach with high risk because health information could be inferred. He fined the company PLN 40,000 for failing to notify the breach and reprimanded it for not informing the data subject without undue delay.

The Austrian DSB fined a sole trader who runs a flower shop EUR 1,500 (plus EUR 150 costs) in an administrative penalty decision. Her shop camera recorded passers-by on the pavement from February 2024 to September 2025 without a lawful basis and beyond its purpose. She also posted images of a man on social media with an accusation of theft, which the DSB held was unlawful further processing of criminal-offence data. A separate charge about missing camera signage (Art. 13 GDPR) was dropped, and the decision is final.

DR introduced mandatory login to watch streaming content on DRTV in autumn 2024. After receiving complaints, the Danish DPA opened its own investigation in spring 2025. It found no sufficiently solid basis to criticise the mandatory login under Article 6(1)(e) GDPR. It did criticise DR under the data minimisation principle, because until 5 September 2025 the login page asked users for their name even though DR had acknowledged that real names were not needed. No fine was imposed.

Aktia Pankki Oyj notified the Office of the Data Protection Ombudsman of a breach in its strong electronic identification service on 24 January 2023. For 47 minutes, users logging in at the same time could see each other's name and personal identity code, and some could then see the other person's data in connected e-services. The Sanctions Board imposed an administrative fine of EUR 865,000 on Aktia, in addition to a reprimand from the Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman. The decision finds breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 25(1) and 32(1) and (2) GDPR, and assesses the breach as at least negligent.

The Polish data protection authority opened proceedings of its own motion against a court bailiff after being told that personal data had been disclosed to an unauthorised recipient. The bailiff had neither reported the breach to the authority within 72 hours nor notified the person whose data was disclosed. The President of UODO found infringements of Articles 33(1) and 34(1)-(2) GDPR and imposed two separate fines, PLN 7,700 and PLN 13,200 (PLN 20,900 in total). The bailiff was also ordered to notify the affected person within 3 days with the information required by Article 34(2).

Parents complained that a secondary school published on its website a circular convening an extraordinary class council for disciplinary proceedings against their son, with the pupil's surname in the file name. The Garante found unlawful dissemination of a minor's data without a legal basis (Art. 5(1)(a), 6 GDPR, Art. 2-ter Code) and a failure to appoint a DPO and notify contact details until after the proceedings began (Art. 37(1) and (7)). The complaint-related Art. 12 charge was dropped as the school removed the file promptly in good faith. Two separate fines of EUR 2,000 each were imposed, totalling EUR 4,000, with publication of the order.

In a series of ex officio checks, the Garante found that the Municipality of Avola had not communicated its data protection officer's contact details to the Authority. The municipality replied that the DPO had been appointed in 2019, that contact details were published on its website, and that the omission was an oversight, and it communicated the details only after being notified. The Garante closed the proceedings on the missing DPO appointment and on publication of the contact details, but confirmed the Article 37(7) breach for failing to communicate the details to the Authority. It fined the municipality EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A former employee of a small municipality complained that CCTV footage and a video filmed by a private individual on the mayor's instruction were used against her in disciplinary proceedings, and that the municipality's CCTV system lacked proper signage and compliance. The Garante found unlawful processing on two separate conducts: street CCTV without a valid legal basis, proper information notices or a DPIA, and use of video in the employment context for disciplinary purposes without labour-law safeguards, including investigative filming outside working hours. It imposed fines of EUR 5,000 and EUR 10,000, totalling EUR 15,000, and ordered publication. No further corrective measures were ordered since the conduct had ceased and the municipality said it had taken remedial steps.

The mayor of an Italian municipality published on his personal Facebook page, and on a second page with the same name, posts naming residents who had tested positive for COVID-19, including minors, and photos and names of 27 children under 12 being vaccinated. He said the people concerned or their parents asked for the posts. The Garante found no valid legal basis under the GDPR or the Italian Privacy Code, and that the processing of health data and minors' data was unlawful. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A complainant received many unwanted promotional SMS messages from a hotel company from 2021 until 2024, despite repeated requests to stop. The company had relied on legitimate interest and on data collected in 2015, and said a 'mishap' prevented the objection from being recorded in its CRM. The Garante found that SMS marketing requires consent, that the deletion request was not properly handled, and fined the company EUR 6,000. The retention period issue was not sanctioned because the company reset it to 5 years. The decision is to be published and noted in the internal register.

A man complained that an online news article about his criminal conviction was still available long after the events, and that the publisher ignored his request of August 2024 to exercise his rights. The publisher's website had no privacy policy or contact details, and the publisher also ignored the Garante's request for information. The article was de-indexed and a privacy policy was published only after proceedings began. The Garante found violations of Article 12(1), (2) and (3) GDPR and Article 157 of the Italian Code, ordered the publisher to put in place measures to facilitate data subject requests, and fined it EUR 20,000.

A person complained that the Latina Bar Association's website published a court hearing schedule PDF containing personal data of the complainant and others, including data on criminal offences and proceedings. The PDF, listing 18 defendants and 4 defence lawyers, stayed online and was indexed by search engines for a long period. The Bar Association blamed human error during the Covid-19 emergency. The Garante found the processing unlawful, lacking a legal basis and breaching the lawfulness principle and Article 10, and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000. No further corrective measures were ordered because the online dissemination had ended.

The DPA fined the Italian public broadcast €150,000 for airing a private conversation of a former Minister involved in a political scandal. The DPA held that broadcasting the conversation was not essential to the journalistic activities of the controller.

The Romanian authority completed an investigation into Agency for Control of Outstanding Debts S.R.L. after a data subject complained. It found that the company could not show it had sent a proper and complete reply to an access request within the legal deadline, and that it did not provide a copy of the requested voice recordings or the reasons for refusing the request. The company was fined 10,192 lei, stated to be the equivalent of EUR 2,000, and was ordered to send a complete reply with the copy and to bring its processing and staff training into line with the GDPR.

IMY examined the Moderate Party's mailing of personalised video greetings before the 2022 Swedish general election. The recipients' data were obtained from referrals and from a commercial database, and the party relied on legitimate interest. IMY found that the party had no legal basis under Article 6(1) because the processing was not necessary and the balancing test failed, and that the information given to recipients under Article 14 was insufficient. No fine was imposed; the party received a reprimand because the infringement was considered minor.

The DPA found that the Sweden Democrats unlawfully sent text messages advertising for votes in an upcoming election. Amongst other things, the political party failed to inform data subjects about the processing of their data.

ANSPDCP concluded an investigation in September 2025 into the electricity producer and supplier Hidroelectrica, started after the company notified a personal data breach. A technical error in the IT system used to send invoices caused a customer to receive an invoice belonging to another person, so several customers' data were disclosed without authorisation. The authority found a breach of Article 32(1)(b) and (d) and (4) GDPR and fined the company RON 25,392 (about EUR 5,000).

The Romanian data protection authority finished an investigation into PRIME TRANSACTION SA in September 2025, started after the company notified a personal data breach. A cyberattack on 9-10 June 2025 gave unauthorised access to the personal data of a significant number of people, including identity document copies and account statements. The authority found that the company had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures and had not regularly tested and assessed their effectiveness. It found a breach of Article 32(1)(b) and (d) and (2) GDPR and fined the company RON 10,162.2, stated as equivalent to EUR 2,000.

Experian Nederland, a credit information bureau, offered a Credit Check service until 1 January 2025 that supplied creditworthiness scores on consumers to its clients. In a primary decision of 6 December 2023 the AP fined it for lacking a valid legal basis (legitimate interest) and for not informing data subjects adequately, and also imposed two penalty orders. On objection, the AP upheld the objection formally, revoked the primary decision and imposed a new fine of EUR 2,700,000 for the same infringements. Experian acknowledged the infringement, stopped its Dutch activities and will delete its database; the press release says it will not appeal.

The DPA imposed a combined £14,000,000 fine on a business services provider and its processor, following a cyber attack which gave unauthorised parties access to over 6 million people’s data. The DPA found a lack of appropriate security measures.

The DPA held that a credit information agency failed to provide a data subject access to the logic involved in its automated credit scoring and to sources and recipients of the data subject’s personal data.

A complainant asked the publisher Delfi Meedia AS to remove their photos from articles published about them over 20 years ago and to replace their name with characters, and got no reply. After the Data Protection Inspectorate raised the matter, Delfi deindexed the articles but refused to remove or pseudonymise the data. The Inspectorate found that public interest had faded, that continued identifiable publication was disproportionate, and that the erasure request should be granted. It issued a binding order to remove the photos and replace the name with initials or other characters by 27 October 2025. No fine was imposed.

Two data subjects complained that Nura OÜ had not provided their treatment data after their access requests under Article 15 GDPR. After repeated unanswered inquiries and a missed summons, the Estonian DPA issued a binding order (ettekirjutus-hoiatus). The order requires Nura OÜ to give each complainant a copy of the treatment outcome and scan files, or explain under Article 12(4) why it will not, and to send the DPA a copy of its replies by 27.10.2025.

ANSPDCP concluded an investigation in September 2025 into an online shop operator, Vellea Home SRL, which had notified a personal data breach after a cyber attack gave unauthorised access to customers' contact data. The authority found that the operator lacked technical and organisational measures appropriate to the risk, breaching Article 32(1)(b) and (2) GDPR. It fined the operator RON 25,376 (about EUR 5,000) and ordered it to revise and update its security incident response plan, including early threat detection and automated alerts through periodic system scanning. This is a press release, not the full decision.

The DPA fined a bank €500,000 for losing a customer’s documents when transporting them via a courier. The DPA held that the bank failed to ensure adequate security and proper supervision of its processor under Article 32 GDPR.

A complainant, who was himself later elected as an alderman in the municipality, complained that the municipality's contact details of internal and external correspondents were used for direct marketing. The mayor, who co-wrote a book, e-mailed those correspondents from the municipal system to invite them to a paid book presentation, and the Litigation Chamber found that the mayor was a separate controller with no lawful basis and no transparency. The Chamber also found that the municipality had given its data protection officer too few resources between November 2023 and December 2024, and it issued a reprimand both to the mayor, for the e-mail, and to the municipality. The complainant had withdrawn the complaint, but the Chamber decided to examine it anyway as supervisory authority.

A daughter complained that a hospital did not give her the medical cause of death of her late father. She had asked by three emails in 2025. The DSB held that these emails were not a request for access under Article 15 GDPR, and that the GDPR does not protect a deceased person's data or let the daughter exercise his right. The complaint was dismissed as unfounded. No fine was imposed.

The DPA held that an event organiser violated a customer’s right to privacy when it submitted them marketing emails without their prior consent and by sending them those emails in CC, disclosing their address to a large group of third parties.

The Romanian authority concluded an investigation into an energy supplier that had notified a personal data breach under Article 33. Customer account data (email addresses and passwords) of a significant number of people had been accessed without authorisation and exfiltrated. The authority found the company lacked appropriate technical and organisational security measures, in breach of Article 32(1)(b) and (2) GDPR. It fined the company 126,797 lei (about EUR 25,000) and ordered it to make multi-factor authentication mandatory for all users and to adopt other suitable security measures.

A health professional complained that the professional Order kept her disciplinary suspension on its online register after she had appealed to the central appeals commission, although the appeal suspends the measure. The Garante found the online publication had no legal basis, breached lawfulness and accuracy principles, and that the Order had not validly designated a Data Protection Officer or notified the Authority of the DPO's contact details. The complaint about sharing data with the national Federation was dismissed. The Garante fined the Order EUR 3,000 for each of the two conducts (EUR 6,000 total), ordered it to designate and publish a DPO and report back within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

A nurse complained that the professional register published on the website of the Pisa nursing order showed every member's home address. The order first claimed the publication was lawful under the sector rules, then said an employee had mistakenly uploaded the full internal register instead of the reduced one, which was also indexed by search engines. The Garante found the processing unlawful for lack of a legal basis and breach of the lawfulness principle, since publishing home addresses was not necessary. It fined the order EUR 16,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures since the conduct had ceased.

Two municipal employee unions reported to the Authority that a CCTV system had been installed at the municipal vehicle depot in Moschato-Tavros and was allegedly used to monitor workers. After several exchanges and a hearing, the Authority found breaches of data minimisation, accountability, data protection by design, transparency and information duties, and of the records of processing requirement. It imposed two fines, EUR 7,000 and EUR 3,000 (EUR 10,000 in total), and a reprimand for Article 30.

A company that runs a website selling lists of phone numbers to estate agents and debt collectors for marketing, was inspected by the Garante after complaints about unwanted calls. The company had labelled itself a processor, but the Garante found it was an independent controller. It had bought lists from an Irish provider without checking consent, processed inaccurate data, ignored data subject requests, gave poor transparency and used a wrong legal basis, and had weak access controls. The Garante banned further processing without valid consent, ordered several corrective measures, and fined the company EUR 5,000, also ordering publication of the decision.

The Garante opened an inquiry of its own motion into Squeezemind s.r.l., a Palermo company, and its use of cookies and its cookie-analysis tool. An inspection in October 2024 found a cookie consent banner and privacy notice that described tracking the company said it had stopped in 2022, and the banner stored users' consent choices in a cookie. The Garante found violations of Articles 5(1)(a) and (c), 12 and 13 GDPR and of Article 122 of the Italian Privacy Code, and issued a reprimand and an order to update the legal documentation and state its update date. No fine was imposed, given the company's cooperation, lack of prior infringements and remedial steps; the Garante dropped its charges about the language used for the website and legal documents and about how the cookie-analysis service was presented.

A company (A***clinics GmbH) complained that a property company had linked an internal extension of the respondent with the name of the company's managing director, alleging breaches of Articles 5, 6, 13 and 16 GDPR. The DSB held that a legal person is not protected by the GDPR (only by § 1 DSG), so the GDPR-based complaint lacked standing and was rejected. The managing director as a natural person may file her own complaint.

The DPA found Microsoft, the school, and the Ministry of Education in violation of information obligations under the GDPR. They also found unlawful processing of non-essential tracking cookies, ordering immediate deletion of data relating to cookies.
The DPA reprimanded a company for unlawfully retaining a former employee’s email account and phone number after the employment ended.

A former member, who had been permanently barred from the controller's premises for repeated house-rule breaches, asked the controller to erase his personal data. The controller kept only his name, surname and date of birth to enforce the ban, relying on legitimate interests under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR. The Slovenian Information Commissioner found no violation of Article 17 GDPR at the time the complaint was lodged, rejected the complaint, and ordered no measures. No costs were awarded.

The Estonian Data Protection Inspectorate opened an own-initiative case against Zu Disain OÜ, a wholesale trading company, which had run an automated script querying the e-land register by person code. The company did not reply to the Inspectorate's proposal or follow-up and gave no legal basis for the processing. The Inspectorate found no valid legal basis, notably no legitimate interest analysis, and issued a binding precept ordering deletion of the personal data collected in this way, or a documented legal basis with a legitimate interest analysis, by 20.10.2025. No fine was imposed; a penalty payment of EUR 2,000 is only threatened if the precept is not complied with.

A complaint about a courier who disclosed a recipient's name and surname to another company led the Spanish AEPD to open sanction proceedings against SEUR GEOPOST, S.L. The AEPD found that SEUR had no data processing contract with CITIBOX (Article 28 GDPR) and that its courier breached confidentiality (Article 5(1)(f) GDPR). SEUR paid voluntarily and got the 20% reduction, so the reduced fine is EUR 164,000, and it must show within 3 months that it has signed a processor contract with CITIBOX.

The DPA reprimanded a public authority for failing to ensure that international personal data transfers complied with the requirements in Chapter V of the GDPR, ordering proper assessment and safeguards.

The Italian DPA investigated ClothOff, an AI 'deep nude' service that turns photos of clothed people into nude images, operated by AI/Robotics Venture Strategy 3 Ltd. The company did not answer a request for information within 30 days. The Garante found the processing unlawful for breaching the principles of fairness and accountability and data protection by design, because age checks and the watermark on generated images were not effective. It also ordered an urgent temporary limitation of processing of Italian users' data. No fine is imposed in this document.

The Hamburg data protection authority fined a financial-sector company EUR 492,000 for infringing customers' rights in automated individual decisions. Credit card applications of several customers with good creditworthiness were rejected by algorithm without human involvement. When the customers asked for reasons, the company did not adequately meet its information and access duties, including meaningful information on the logic involved. The company's extensive efforts to improve its process and its full cooperation were weighed as substantially mitigating, and it accepted the fine notice. The release also gives a mid-year summary of fines in 2025, totalling about EUR 775,000, including a separate EUR 195,000 fine on a retail company.

This is a mid-year press release from the Hamburg DPA covering several fines issued in 2025, totalling about EUR 775,000. The part matching this Fino entry concerns a retail company that hired service providers to send postal advertising and, in several cases and over a longer period, failed to answer data subjects' rights requests on time. The authority fined it EUR 195,000. The release also describes a EUR 492,000 fine against a financial company over non-transparent automated decisions, plus smaller fines for email advertising without consent and for employees' unauthorised database look-ups.

A customer's satisfaction survey was sent by e-mail in eight identical messages to about 450 recipients, with all addresses visible in the cc field, which the complainant reported. The Litigation Chamber treated the matter as a prima facie decision under Article 95 WOG. It issued a warning to the controller to take sufficient technical and organisational measures to secure personal data (Articles 5(1)(f), 25 and 32 GDPR) in future. It dismissed the complaint on opportunity grounds as far as the breach notification duties (Articles 33 and 34 GDPR) were concerned. No fine was imposed.

A data subject complained that a savings bank refused to have a loan-payment entry removed from a credit register after a 2017 court judgment, arguing the claim was forfeited and that the entry dated from 2014. The authority held that Austrian law has no general forfeiture by inaction, that the 30-year limitation period had not run, and that the debt remained outstanding and still creditworthiness-relevant, so Article 17 GDPR did not require erasure. The complaint was dismissed as unfounded.

The Austrian DSB newsletter 3/2025 summarises a penalty decision of 29 September 2025 against a person using a Tesla with a seven-camera system. The cameras recorded in real time and automatically saved footage when suspicious movement was detected while parked. This captured people near the vehicle regardless of security incidents, stored the footage for over a month, and the people were not informed. The DSB found breaches of Art. 5(1)(a), (c), (e), Art. 6(1), Art. 12 and 13 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 600. The decision is not final.

The DPA held that a credit information agency violated the prohibition of automated individual decision-making (ADM) by calculating a data subject’s creditworthiness leading to an energy provider’s decision not to conclude a contract with the data subject. The energy provider’s rejection also constituted ADM but was considered necessary for entering into a contract.

Following a personal data breach notification, the Romanian authority investigated an e-commerce operator whose platform was hit by a cyberattack exposing customers' payment card data. It found the site ran an outdated version of its platform without adequate security measures. The operator was fined RON 101,544 (about EUR 20,000) for breaching Article 32 GDPR. It was also ordered to implement a logging system for all access to its e-commerce platform, with backups of the logs. The operator has paid the fine.

A former employee of the municipality complained, through her lawyer, that two municipal council resolutions containing her personal data, including references to a criminal proceeding against her, remained published on the municipality's website. The municipality admitted that the publication resulted from human error because the publishing officer did not receive the confidentiality alert, and the resolutions were online for 15 days. The Garante found unlawful processing of personal data (Articles 5(1)(a), 6 and 10 GDPR), and a failure to answer the erasure request within the deadline (Articles 12(3) and (4), 17 GDPR), and imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 for all the violations together.

A real estate agency affiliated with Tecnocasa sent two unsolicited promotional emails to a property owner without consent. It ignored his erasure request and gave only vague answers to the Garante, claiming errors and oversights. The company had already been reprimanded and ordered in 2021 for similar conduct, and had not complied. The Garante found violations of Article 6(1)(a), Articles 12(3) and 17 and Article 58(2)(d) GDPR, and fined the company EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.

The DPA fined the Province of Bolzano €32,000 for unlawfully operating a network of cameras monitoring traffic flows. The province had no valid legal basis for the involved processing of personal data, in particular license plates.

An employee complained that the company had created a work email account in his name without telling him, and that the account was used by many other people. The Garante found that the account, active from October 2019 to February 2023, was in practice a shared account used by employees and logistics contractors. It found breaches of the data protection principles and of the lawfulness and information duties, closed the allegations on Articles 25 and 32, ordered the company to prepare compliant information documents on corporate email accounts, and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000.

The Garante had already issued corrective decision n. 297/2021 against the Comune di Pazzano (a very small municipality) and ordered it to publish its DPO contact details and to answer an information request within 30 days. The Comune did not comply on time, and its website privacy notice was an empty page lacking the Article 13 information. The Garante found three separate infringements: non-compliance with its order (Art. 58(2)(d) GDPR), failure to answer its information request (Art. 157 Codice), and the deficient notice (Arts. 12 and 13 GDPR). It imposed a total fine of EUR 3,960, split into three fines of EUR 1,320, and ordered publication of the decision, noting that the Comune had since remedied the breaches.

The Italian DPA investigated E-Power S.r.l., an energy/photovoltaic seller, after many complaints about unsolicited promotional calls made without a valid legal basis, including to numbers on the public opposition register, and an unanswered rights request. The company bought contact lists from a Moldovan list provider without checking their origin or consent, wrongly treated roles, and had a deficient website contact form. The Authority dropped the charge on late replies to its information requests, but found the other violations proven. It fined the company EUR 35,000, banned further processing of the complainants' data, ordered compliance measures and ordered publication of the decision.

A former employee asked his ex-employer, Green.mec. s.r.l., for access under Article 15 GDPR in August 2023 to training certificates and the communications behind his dismissal. The company did not reply within the one-month deadline and handed over only part of the documents after the Garante opened an inquiry; the disciplinary documents were still not delivered. The Garante found infringements of Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR, ordered the access to be granted within 30 days, and imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 on Officine Serena s.r.l., the company that absorbed Green.mec.

A hospital employee complained that details of her miscarriage, treated at the hospital where she works, had circulated among colleagues. The complaint pointed to access to the hospital's health dossier through a generic radiology account. The Garante's investigation found that the hospital's health dossier was configured in breach of the basic processing principles, security and privacy by design rules and its 2015 dossier guidelines. It declared the processing unlawful, fined the hospital EUR 20,000 and ordered it to remove the 'pharmacovigilance' access mode and restrict a nursing profile's access. The hospital must also report on its measures within 90 days. The decision is to be published.

Several people complained that a Fanpage.it undercover report, broadcast by La7 and published online by Ciao People S.r.l., used images of a private gathering they attended, filmed by a reporter who had joined under a false name. They asked for the footage to be removed. The Garante declared the complaint unfounded. It found the processing served a legitimate journalistic purpose, that the participants' faces and voices were obscured, and that the complainants had not shown they were recognisable or that the venue was their home. The Tribunal of Naples rejected one challenge and confirmed the decision in full (judgment 5994/2026 of 13 April 2026); another challenge, before the Tribunal of Rome, is pending.

The DPA held that a lawyer, acting as a data controller, lawfully requested user profile data from an online platform and disclosed it in civil proceedings. The processing was justified, as it served the lawyer’s legitimate interests in representing his client.

The Romanian authority investigated Dr.Max SRL after a data subject complained that the company refused her erasure request. The investigation found that the controller did not show it had answered that request, and that an employee had kept a copy of her identity card without her consent. The authority found infringements of Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 17 GDPR, imposed a fine of RON 5,057.8 (stated as EUR 1,000), and ordered corrective measures. The press release says the controller has paid the fine.

After a press article and an employee complaint, the CNIL inspected the Samaritaine department store, which had installed five cameras disguised as smoke detectors, with microphones, in two stockrooms in August 2023 to deal with thefts. The restricted committee found the covert filming and sound recording of employees unfair and undocumented (not in the records or the DPIA, DPO not informed), as well as excessive data collection, and also found breaches of Articles 33(1), 33(5) and 38(1). It described the company's conduct as clearly negligent. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 100,000 and ordered publication, with the company no longer named after two years.

In December 2023 Servicios Financieros Carrefour notified the AEPD of a cyber incident in which an attacker used compromised credentials to extract customer personal data, including financial and payment-related data. The AEPD opened a sanction procedure alleging a breach of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, because appropriate security measures were not in place, and proposed a fine of EUR 2,500,000. The company acknowledged responsibility and paid voluntarily on 27 August 2025, receiving two 20% reductions. The AEPD confirmed the infringement and set the final fine at EUR 1,500,000, ending the procedure.

The Polish DPA fined Q. Sp. z o.o., a therapy and medical services company, for breaching Article 38(6) GDPR. From 16 July 2018 to 4 July 2024 its data protection officer was also the company's management board president, which created a conflict of interest. The case began after the company reported a breach in August 2023 in which a medical certificate was wrongly issued to a patient, and the DPA opened its own proceedings. The DPA found the breach intentional and aggravating, but gave credit for the company ending the conflict in July 2024 by appointing a different DPO, and set the fine at 11,365 PLN (about 2,700 EUR).

The Italian DPA inspected a nursing home in Rome (Casa di Cura Città di Roma) on its electronic health record (dossier sanitario). It found that nurses, doctors and administrative staff could see data of patients well beyond what they needed, including after consent was withdrawn. Read-access logging was missing, with no alerts, no log checks, no penetration tests and no training on the dossier. The Authority declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5, 9, 25 and 32 GDPR and fined the clinic EUR 12,000, treating the seriousness as medium. It ordered no corrective measures because the clinic had already fixed the problems, and it ordered publication of the order.

An employee of the Florence Fire Brigade Command complained that a spreadsheet with colleagues' names, vaccination status and health-related notes was posted on the Command's Telegram channel, which had about 260 members. The Ministry said a staff member posted the file by mistake and removed it after about 5 minutes. The Garante found the processing unlawful, since there was no suitable legal basis and the data went to people not authorised to see it. It fined the Ministry EUR 12,000 and ordered publication of the order. It found no need for further corrective measures.

A candidate for the post of director of a regional park authority complained that the minutes of the selection committee, containing personal data of all 45 candidates, had been published on the authority's website and indexed by search engines. The minutes also included self-declarations about pending criminal proceedings or convictions for seven candidates. The authority said it was a clerical error and removed and de-indexed the documents quickly. The Garante found the disclosure had no legal basis and breached lawfulness principles and the rules on criminal-conviction data. It imposed a fine of EUR 8,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Garante received reports that the Municipality of Buccino had published on its Facebook page many photos of minors and of people with mental disabilities. It also found that the Municipality had not published the contact details of its data protection officer. The Municipality did not follow up the hearing invitation and filed no defence after the supplementary notice. The Garante found breaches of the lawfulness and minimisation principles, the special-category rules, and the DPO publication duties. It fined the Municipality EUR 4,000 for the Facebook publications and EUR 2,000 for the DPO omission, total EUR 6,000, ordered it to stop the dissemination and publish the DPO contact details, and ordered publication of the decision.

Following an inspection by the Guardia di finanza, the Garante found that a company operated video surveillance systems in two shops (3 and 4 cameras) without adequate information signs and without the Labour Inspectorate authorisation required by Article 4 of Law 300/1970. The company filed no defence. The Garante declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR and Article 114 of the Code. It imposed a fine of EUR 6,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A former employee of the municipality of Nichelino complained that her request to rectify two published decisions was not answered. The decisions, which stated she failed her probation, stayed online far too long. The Garante also found that the municipality kept intermediate and final rankings of a public competition online with excessive candidate data. It found breaches of lawfulness, minimisation, legal basis and the data subject's rectification right. It imposed two fines, EUR 10,000 and EUR 8,000, totalling EUR 18,000, and ordered publication of the decision.

A former employee of a fast-food restaurant operator complained that the company did not respond to her requests (8 and 11 June 2024) for training certificates and a medical fitness certificate, and later to a formal access request of 26 August 2024. The company argued it was not obliged to provide certificates issued by her previous employer, and only supplied the documents in January 2025, after the Garante opened its inquiry. The Garante found infringements of Articles 5(1)(a), 12 and 15 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 1,000, taking into account the company's cooperation as a mitigating factor. The order is also to be published on the Garante's website.

The Garante investigated SEA's 'FaceBoarding' facial recognition system used to identify passengers at the security gates and boarding gates at Milan Linate airport. It found that the biometric templates are stored centrally under the airport operator's control, which falls within scenario 3 of EDPB Opinion 11/2024, and that there is no encryption, retention of up to 12 months, template generation for non-enrolled passengers, and an inaccurate privacy notice. The Garante ordered an urgent provisional limitation of the processing of passengers' biometric data through FaceBoarding, and also ordered publication and recording of the measure. No fine was imposed in this measure, and the investigation remained open.

The DPA found that a restaurant owner unlawfully recorded data subjects on a public street and monitored employees and guests without a valid legal basis. The DPA prohibited the continued use of the CCTV system and stressed that any future surveillance must comply with GDPR principles.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in August 2025 into Unita Turism Holding S.A., which had notified a personal data breach under Article 33 GDPR. A cyber attack led to unauthorised disclosure and extraction of data on current and former employees, including national ID numbers, medical and bank/financial documents. The investigation found the controller did not have appropriate technical and organisational security measures in place at the time of the attack. It was fined RON 25,368 (stated as equivalent to EUR 5,000), and the fine has been paid.

The DPA fined a bank €1,800,000 for failing to implement sufficient technical and organisational measures regarding a new login feature on their app, which led to unauthorised access to customers' accounts by third parties.
The DPA issued a warning to a company engaging in direct marketing for failing to respond to a data subject’s requests to access and erasure. The DPA announced a fine in case the violation continues.

The Estonian Data Protection Inspectorate published a press release saying it fined Allium UPI OÜ, the company that runs the Apotheka loyalty programme, EUR 3 million. A security incident in early 2024 let unauthorised persons repeatedly access the information system and a backup of the database, and they downloaded customer data from 2014 to 2020 for more than 750,000 people, including purchase history that points to health. The inspectorate found basic security measures were missing, such as multi-factor authentication and shared administrator accounts. The press release says the decision is not yet in force and can be challenged within 15 days.

This is a newsletter item summarising a penalty decision (Straferkenntnis) of the Austrian DPA of 5 September 2025 against a bakery company. For more than a year the company ran 30 insufficiently signposted video cameras across several bakery sites, covering customer areas, public areas and staff-only areas, and the settings were not the least intrusive means in time or place. Passers-by, customers and employees were filmed without a justifying basis. In at least one case footage was also passed on via a messenger service, contrary to the purpose-limitation rule. The authority imposed a fine of EUR 33,500; the decision is not yet final.

A tenant complained to the Belgian DPA about the unlawful use of four surveillance cameras in and around a student house. After an inspection, the Litigation Chamber found the landlord had no valid legal basis for the cameras, breached the accountability principle, filmed the public road and neighbours' property (data minimisation) and kept no processing register. It ordered the cameras switched off and the data deleted, issued a reprimand for the missing register, and imposed fines of EUR 8,000 and EUR 1,200 plus a EUR 500 increase for aggravating circumstances, totalling EUR 9,700. The transparency complaint was rejected.

Following data breach notifications from its processor Stratesys and controller SAREB after a cyberattack, the Spanish DPA investigated security failures and the lack of a compliant data processing agreement. The AEPD found that SAREB breached Article 5(1)(f) GDPR due to insufficient technical and organizational security measures and excessive data retention, as well as Article 28 GDPR for lacking a compliant data processing agreement with Stratesys. SAREB acknowledged its responsibility and made voluntary payment of the proposed fines, benefiting from two cumulative 20% statutory reductions that reduced the initial penalty of EUR 300,000 to EUR 180,000. In its final decision, the AEPD terminated the proceedings, confirmed the EUR 180,000 fine, and ordered SAREB to demonstrate compliance with security measures and Article 28 requirements within three months.

An Austrian advertising agency left a development server subdomain exposing a file directory with personal data (names, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, phone numbers, company affiliation, postcodes). A first warning in January 2025 was treated as spam by an employee and not escalated. After a second warning on 16 February 2025, copied to the DSB, management acted and closed the gap, but the company did not notify the DSB itself until 2 May 2025. The DSB found a breach of the 72-hour notification duty in Art. 33(1) GDPR, negligently committed, and imposed a fine of EUR 870 plus EUR 87 in costs.

The Danish High Court (Vestre Landsret) fined ILVA A/S DKK 1.5 million for breaching the GDPR rules on storage limitation, which the Danish Data Protection Authority had proposed. The breach was that an older IT system holding customer data had no deletion deadlines or deletion procedures. The court calculated the fine on the group's total net turnover, following a 13 February 2025 CJEU ruling (C-383/23) on the meaning of 'undertaking'. The court also found the breach intentional because management knew the facts.

A data subject complained that the controller kept processing her email address for mailing purposes after her membership of an association ended, and that it ignored her objections to marketing. The Commissioner found that the controller had no legal basis under Article 6(1) for keeping her address on the list of people who receive forwarded messages after her membership ended, which violated the lawfulness principle in Article 5(1)(a). The marketing-objection complaint was not proven, because the messages were personal messages from individuals rather than the controller's newsletters. The controller had already removed her address before the decision, so no corrective order was made, and no fine was imposed.

Following two CNIL inspection missions (2022 and 2023) on Gmail and on advertising cookies placed when creating a Google account, the restricted committee found that Google LLC and Google Ireland Limited breached Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act (cookies placed without valid consent, with an account-creation path biased towards accepting targeted advertising) and Article L. 34-5 of the postal and electronic communications code (ads inserted between Gmail emails without prior consent). It fined Google LLC EUR 200,000,000 and Google Ireland Limited EUR 125,000,000, using the Alphabet group turnover as the economic-unit basis. It also ordered both companies to comply, with a EUR 100,000 per day penalty after six months, and ordered publication of the decision.

A Norwegian complainant's OneDrive account was suspended by Microsoft in February 2020 after child sexual abuse material was detected on it. Microsoft later deleted the data and refused the complainant's access request, relying on Article 15(4) GDPR. The DPC, as lead authority, found infringements of Article 5(1)(a) and Article 12(4) GDPR. It issued a reprimand and ordered Microsoft to revise its user-facing policies on retention, permanent deletion and appeals, but imposed no administrative fine.

After a cyber-attack, La Fântâna S.R.L. notified a personal data breach to the Romanian authority. The investigation, finished in July 2025, found that the company did not have appropriate technical and organisational security measures in place when the attack happened. Card data of a significant number of people was disclosed, creating a risk of bank fraud. The company was fined RON 50,693 (about EUR 10,000) and has already paid it.

Following an online inspection of the shein.com website on 10 August 2023, the CNIL restricted committee found that the company placed advertising and other cookies on users' terminals without prior consent. It also found that refusal and withdrawal of consent were not effective and that consent was not informed because the third parties placing advertising cookies were not identified. The committee used the turnover of the parent company, as the economic unit, to set the fine. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 150 million and ordered publication of the decision, which will no longer name the company after two years. No injunction was issued because the company had come into compliance during the proceedings.
The DPA fined a company €5,000 for calling a data subject for direct marketing purposes without their consent, in violation of national telecommunication laws.

The Polish DPA published news that it fined ING Bank Śląski PLN 18,416,400 for scanning identity documents of customers and prospective customers between 1 April 2019 and 23 September 2020. The bank did not assess whether scanning was necessary under AML rules and scanned documents even for matters such as ATM complaints. The President of UODO found a lack of legal basis and breaches of the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation and data minimisation. The fine was considered effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

The Belgian DPA's Dispute Chamber found that a bicycle rental company had unlawfully processed a complainant's identity card image, uploaded to a third-party verifier for fraud checks, because no legal basis applied, including legitimate interest, which failed the necessity test. It also found transparency breaches about the identity card processing and about possible continuous location tracking of rented bikes, and a breach for not answering an access request within one month.
